title: Preparing features

sections.title: 8.3 It really does matter: an experiment

html:
Purpose. A model only sees the numbers you give it. The same data, rescaled or combined in a smarter way, can train in 70 steps instead of never, and can fit a curve with a linear model. This chapter is about turning raw columns into good inputs.

Key ideas

  • Features on very different scales make gradient descent slow. Rescale them to similar ranges, roughly -1 to +1.
  • Fit the scaling on the training data only and reuse its numbers for new data.
  • Feature engineering builds new inputs from old ones: ratios, products, powers, dates, one-hot columns.
  • Adding powers of a feature (x, x squared, x cubed) lets a linear model fit a curve. Scaling then matters even more.

8.1 Why scaling matters

Suppose size runs from 300 to 2,000 square feet and bedrooms from 0 to 5. Take a 2,000 sq ft house with 5 bedrooms that costs $500k (Ng, video 25):

  • w1 = 50, w2 = 0.1, b = 50 predicts 50 x 2000 + 0.1 x 5 + 50, over $100 million. Terrible.
  • w1 = 0.1, w2 = 50, b = 50 predicts 0.1 x 2000 + 50 x 5 + 50 = 500, which is $500k. Right.

So a feature with a big range ends up with a small weight, and a feature with a small range ends up with a big weight. That has a consequence for the cost surface:

When the features differ in scale, the cost contours are long thin ovals: a tiny change in w1 changes the cost a lot, and a big change in w2 barely changes it. Gradient descent bounces across the narrow valley and crawls along it. After scaling, the contours are close to circles and the path goes almost straight to the minimum. (The picture is a simple bowl drawn to show the idea.)

8.2 Three ways to rescale

Ng's numbers: size has mean 600 and standard deviation 450, bedrooms have mean 2.3 and standard deviation 1.4.

Method Formula Size (300 to 2000) becomes Bedrooms (0 to 5) becomes
Divide by the maximum x / max 0.15 to 1 0 to 1
Mean normalization (x - mean) / (max - min) -0.18 to 0.82 -0.46 to 0.54
Z-score normalization (x - mean) / standard deviation -0.67 to 3.1 -1.6 to 1.9
xjscaled=xj−μjσjx_j^{\text{scaled}} = \frac{x_j - \mu_j}{\sigma_j}

Rule of thumb: aim for roughly -1 to +1 per feature. Anything from -3 to 3 or from -0.3 to 0.3 is fine. A feature from -100 to 100, one from -0.001 to 0.001, or body temperature at 98.6 to 105 degrees (all around 100) should be rescaled. There is almost never any harm in rescaling, so when in doubt, do it.

Fit on training data only. Compute the mean and standard deviation from the training rows, and reuse those same numbers on validation, test and production data (Chapter 3). In scikit-learn that is StandardScaler().fit(X_train) and then .transform(...) for every set.

8.3 It really does matter: an experiment

Here is synthetic housing data built from a known recipe (price = 0.1 x size + 50 x bedrooms + 50, plus noise), fitted with the function from Chapter 7:

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
size = rng.uniform(300, 2000, 200)
beds = rng.integers(0, 6, 200).astype(float)
y = 0.1 * size + 50 * beds + 50 + rng.normal(0, 10, 200)
X = np.c_[size, beds]

mu, sd = X.mean(axis=0), X.std(axis=0)
Z = (X - mu) / sd                                   # z-score each column
w, b, h = gradient_descent(Z, y, alpha=0.1, steps=300)
print(int(np.argmax(h <= h[-1] * 1.001)) + 1)        # 68  steps to get within 0.1% of the final cost
print(round(h[-1], 2))                               # 39.11  final cost with scaling

w2, b2, h2 = gradient_descent(X, y, alpha=1e-6, steps=300)   # unscaled
print(round(h2[-1]))                                 # 5905  cost WITHOUT scaling after 300 steps

With scaling, gradient descent is done in 68 steps and the cost is 39. Without scaling it is still at 5,905 after 300 steps, and it cannot use a bigger alpha, because any alpha above about 1.3e-6 makes it diverge. Same data, same model.

Reading the weights after scaling. The weights from the scaled run are in scaled units. To get back to dollars per square foot, divide each by its standard deviation, and adjust b:

print(np.round(w / sd, 3), round(b - np.sum(w * mu / sd), 2))   # [ 0.101 50.265] 48.96
A = np.c_[X, np.ones(len(y))]
print(np.round(np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)[0], 3))       # [ 0.101 50.265 48.964]  the exact answer

The recipe was 0.1, 50 and 50, and both methods recover it up to the noise. Scaling changes how fast training is, not what it finds.

8.4 Feature engineering

Choosing or inventing the right features is often the biggest lever on quality (Ng, video 29). The idea: use what you know about the problem to combine or transform the raw columns so the pattern is easier to learn.

  • Products and ratios. Ng's example: lot frontage x1 and depth x2 are less useful than their product x3 = x1 x2, the area. In lending: debt to income, loan to value, amount per term (amount divided by number of terms).
  • Dates. A date becomes day of week, month, days since the account opened, days until the due date.
  • Skewed numbers. Amounts and incomes are often skewed: a few huge values. Taking the logarithm often helps.
  • Categories as numbers. A model needs numbers, so a category like loan purpose becomes one-hot columns: one 0 or 1 column per category. Do not number categories 1, 2, 3, because that would imply that home (3) is three times car (1).
  • Missing values and outliers. Fill missing values with the median and add a column that says the value was missing; look at the extreme values before deciding whether they are errors or real.
import pandas as pd

offers = pd.DataFrame({
    "OfferedAmount": [10000, 25000, 5000],
    "NumberOfTerms": [36, 60, 24],
    "Purpose": ["car", "home", "car"],
})
offers["AmountPerTerm"] = (offers["OfferedAmount"] / offers["NumberOfTerms"]).round(1)
offers = pd.get_dummies(offers, columns=["Purpose"], dtype=int)
print(offers)
#    OfferedAmount  NumberOfTerms  AmountPerTerm  Purpose_car  Purpose_home
# 0          10000             36          277.8            1             0
# 1          25000             60          416.7            0             1
# 2           5000             24          208.3            1             0

8.5 Polynomial regression

A straight line fits curved data badly. The fix is to feed the same linear model extra columns made from powers of the feature (Ng, video 30):

f(x)=w1x+w2x2+w3x3+bf(x) = w_1 x + w_2 x^2 + w_3 x^3 + b

This is still linear regression, because the model is linear in the weights: the features are x, x squared and x cubed, and gradient descent does not care how they were made. Which shape? A quadratic eventually comes back down, which makes no sense for house prices. A cubic rises again for large houses. The square root of x flattens out but never goes down. Pick what fits the world you are modelling.

Scaling is now essential. With size from 1 to 1,000, x squared reaches a million and x cubed a billion:

from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X = np.array([[300.0], [800.0], [1500.0], [2000.0]])           # size in square feet
poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=3, include_bias=False)
print(poly.fit_transform(X).max(axis=0))                       # [2.e+03 4.e+06 8.e+09]  the raw ranges
Z = make_pipeline(poly, StandardScaler()).fit_transform(X)     # all three columns now about -1.5 to 1.6

How many powers to use is a question about overfitting, which is the topic of Chapter 11. Choosing features properly, by measuring how well each choice performs on held-out data, comes in Ng's course 2.

Loan example. The offers table has amounts in the thousands and terms in the tens, so scale them before gradient descent. Then add AmountPerTerm and compare the error with and without it. If the new feature helps, the model had a pattern it could not express with the raw columns alone.

Common mistakes

  • Scaling before splitting the data, which leaks test information into training.
  • Not saving the training mean and standard deviation, then scaling new data with different numbers.
  • Turning categories into 1, 2, 3.
  • Adding polynomial features without scaling them.

Check yourself

  • Why does a feature measured in thousands make gradient descent slow?
  • Z-score the value 1000 when the mean is 600 and the standard deviation is 450.
  • Why is polynomial regression still called linear regression?
  • Name two features you could build from the columns OfferedAmount and NumberOfTerms.
Show answers

(1) The weight for that feature must be tiny, and the cost surface becomes a narrow valley that gradient descent zigzags across. (2) (1000 - 600) / 450 = 0.89. (3) Because it is linear in the weights, even though the features are powers of x. (4) AmountPerTerm (amount divided by terms), and the logarithm of the amount.
